lab_title: VSEPR Theory: Predicting Molecular Geometry in 3D
top_level_objectives: Apply VSEPR theory to predict the arrangement of electron domains around a central atom from a Lewis structure
Distinguish between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry when lone pairs are present
Identify and construct the five fundamental electron-domain geometries and their lone-pair-modified shapes
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and predict resulting bond-angle deviations
Compare VSEPR predictions to experimentally observed geometries in real molecules

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the idea that a Lewis structure encodes information about electron domains (bonds and lone pairs) around a central atom, which is the starting point for predicting 3D shape.
key_visuals: A flat 2D Lewis structure of a simple molecule (e.g., water) floating in space
Highlighted bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom in different colors
A transition animation morphing the flat structure into a 3D cloud of electron domains
student_actions: Tap on each bond and lone pair in the Lewis structure to identify it as a domain
Count the total number of electron domains around the central atom
Predict whether the domains are all bonding or include lone pairs

scenes.scene_name: Minimizing Repulsion: The Core VSEPR Principle
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the central VSEPR idea that electron domains push apart to minimize repulsion, establishing the physical reasoning behind molecular shapes.
key_visuals: A generic central atom with movable electron-domain markers (spheres) connected by elastic-looking lines
Domains snapping into evenly spaced arrangements as repulsion is minimized
A repulsion-force visualization (glowing rings) shrinking as domains spread apart
student_actions: Drag electron domain markers around the central atom and observe repulsion forces update in real time
Release the domains and watch them settle into the lowest-energy arrangement
Compare an unminimized arrangement to the settled one and note the difference in angles

scenes.brief_purpose: Walk students through the five basic geometries (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral) that arise purely from the number of electron domains, before lone pairs are considered.
key_visuals: Five separate 3D scaffolds, each showing 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 domains arranged symmetrically
Idealized bond angles labeled on each geometry (180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°/120°, 90°)
Rotatable central-atom models for each geometry
student_actions: Select each of the five domain counts and rotate the resulting geometry to inspect it from all angles
Match each geometry to its idealized bond angle by tapping the correct label
Record how the geometry changes as one more domain is added

scenes.scene_name: Introducing Lone Pairs: From Electron-Domain to Molecular Geometry
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how replacing one or more bonding domains with lone pairs changes the observed molecular shape while the underlying electron-domain arrangement stays the same.
key_visuals: A tetrahedral electron-domain scaffold with one domain highlighted as a lone pair (shown as a shaded lobe instead of a bond)
Side-by-side comparison of electron-domain geometry versus molecular geometry (bonds only)
Progressive examples: tetrahedral to trigonal pyramidal to bent as lone pairs are added
student_actions: Toggle domains between 'bonding pair' and 'lone pair' and observe the resulting molecular shape
Name the molecular geometry produced at each lone-pair count for a given electron-domain geometry
Sketch or select the correct shape name from a list for each configuration

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pair vs Bonding Pair Repulsion and Bond-Angle Deviation
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, causing compression of bond angles below the idealized values, using water and methane as contrasting examples.
key_visuals: Side-by-side methane (109.5°, all bonding pairs) and water (104.5°, two lone pairs) models
Angular 'size' of lone pair electron clouds shown larger and more diffuse than bonding pair clouds
Animated compression of the H-O-H angle from 109.5° down to 104.5° as lone pair repulsion is applied
student_actions: Measure and compare the bond angle in methane versus water using an on-screen angle tool
Adjust a repulsion-strength slider for lone pairs and observe how the bond angle shrinks accordingly
Explain in a short response why lone pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair repulsion

scenes.scene_name: Building Real Molecules: Matching VSEPR to Observed Structures
scenes.brief_purpose: Let students apply the full VSEPR workflow to real molecules, reinforcing the connection between predicted and experimentally observed geometries.
key_visuals: A gallery of real molecule models: H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, XeF4
Each molecule shown first as a Lewis structure, then morphing into its 3D VSEPR-predicted shape
Labels showing molecular geometry name and idealized vs actual bond angle for each
student_actions: Select a molecule from the gallery and build its Lewis structure by placing bonds and lone pairs
Predict the molecular geometry before revealing the 3D model to check the prediction
Compare predicted bond angles to literature values displayed for each molecule

scenes.brief_purpose: Assess understanding by having students independently determine the geometry of new, unseen molecules using the full VSEPR process without guided prompts.
key_visuals: A set of unlabeled Lewis structures for unfamiliar molecules or ions (e.g., ClF3, BrF5, SO2)
An empty 3D workspace where students must construct the geometry from scratch
A feedback panel that reveals the correct geometry and bond angles after submission
student_actions: Count electron domains and classify each as bonding or lone pair for a new molecule
Construct the predicted 3D molecular geometry by placing domains in the workspace
Submit the final shape and compare it against the revealed correct structure for feedback
